title: Joe Petit's trombone and leaving Mollier for the boat
summary: Russell's recording of Petit with Wooden Joe, his one-tooth embouchure, and Mollier's blessing for the boat job.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: And one time, uh, I, I made a record. He, uh, a friend of me, of mine told me that he'd once expressed the wish to make a record. So once when I was recording, uh, Bunk Johnson and, uh, this happened to be Wooden Joe's band. Yeah, he made these with Wooden Joe, Nicholas. Uh huh. And, um, uh, Burbank. And we had him just, he didn't even have his trombone. He'd given up trombone. He used Jim Robinson's trombone. A couple of numbers played Careless Love and St. Louis Blues. He was quite deaf. He had trouble first hearing what key they were in. Yes. He had tried a couple of times and he got onto it. Without any teeth, too. No teeth, but he still doesn't play.

That's right, because when, I can remember that was something else that I remember about him. When he was playing the trombone when, uh, we were with Paul Moyer's group, he had one tooth on the side. It was the, the eye, the eye tooth. And he would place it on the side of the eye tooth and would brace his lip for his embouchure. A strong lip. And he played.
Even when he hadn't played for years, he, after ten minutes time, he'd fill the horn.

And, um, when I was called to play with the, with the group on the boat, uh, I gave due respect to, uh, Mr. Mollier and told him that, uh, that opportunity was presenting myself. And he said he felt proud of me and that he wanted to see me make it. Because at that time, musicians, they seemingly had, um, they had a mania for playing on the boat. And two, they felt that when you played on the boat that you had been given quite a bit of recognition because we'd always had good bands.
Yeah, he got to travel and see a little bit of the country there too, I guess. Yeah.
